children: For Neha Mishra, the fixed deposit she opened in her own name in 2025 was meant to remain her money. But after her husband’s death, that deposit became the source from which the State Bank of India (SBI) recovered nearly Rs 20 lakh towards his outstanding personal loan.

The Allahabad High Court has now ordered SBI to return the entire amount, along with interest, and pay Mishra Rs 1 lakh as compensation, while strongly criticising the manner in which the bank carried out the debit, in an 8-page order dated September 10, seen by
Moneycontrol
A loan taken by her husband
Mishra’s husband, an Assistant Professor at Medicine Hospital in Lucknow, had taken a Rs 15 lakh Xpress Credit Loan from SBI on November 3, 2020.

Mishra herself had no role in that loan agreement. The court noted that she had neither signed the loan documents nor agreed to be associated with the borrowing as a co-applicant, co-borrower, guarantor, surety, indemnifier or nominee.
The bench of Justice Shekhar B Saraf and Justice Abdhesh Kumar Chaudhary therefore found that there was no contractual relationship between Mishra and SBI in connection with the loan.
The loan had also been covered by insurance arranged through SBI General Insurance. The court recorded that Mishra’s husband had allegedly paid a premium of Rs 8,803 for that cover.
He died of Covid-19 on May 6, 2021.
SBI sought payment from the widow
After his death, the bank pursued Mishra for the outstanding loan. A legal notice issued on September 23, 2025, demanded Rs 13,87,382 plus interest.
Before that, on September 12, 2025, SBI had placed Mishra’s salary account on hold. She approached the Reserve Bank of India Ombudsman, following which the hold was removed.
The dispute then moved into negotiations between the parties. During this period, however, SBI encashed a fixed deposit belonging to Mishra and debited Rs 19,90,693 from her account.

The FD had been opened by Mishra at SBI’s Ashiyana branch in 2025. The bank transferred the account to its Jankipuram branch, where her husband had originally taken the loan. The amount was then deducted and transferred towards the loan dues. The account was subsequently moved back to Ashiyana.
Why the court rejected SBI’s defence
SBI relied on a standing instruction signed by Mishra’s husband when he took the loan.

Under that instruction, he had authorised the bank to receive amounts payable towards provident fund, gratuity, pension and similar dues if his employment ended through retirement, resignation, termination or other discontinuation. The authorisation was stated to remain in force until the loan was cleared.
SBI also cited earlier judgments concerning recovery of loan dues from gratuity and other retiral benefits.

But the High Court said those cases dealt with different circumstances. Here, the money had been taken from a bank account belonging to a third party -- Mishra -- and SBI was not her husband’s employer.
The court also noted that there was no material establishing that the money taken from Mishra’s FD represented gratuity or another retiral benefit received after her husband’s death.
'A serious breach of trust'
The judges questioned SBI’s lawyer on whether the same recovery method could have been used if Mishra’s account had been with another bank. The answer was no.
The court said SBI appeared to have been able to make the deduction because Mishra’s FD was held with SBI itself.
The judgment observed that the bank had “merely debited the bank account of the petitioner, as the petitioner had a fixed deposit in the respondent-Bank.”
The bench described this as “a serious breach of trust reposed on the Banks”, noting that banks act as custodians of customers’ money.
Court orders refund and compensation
The judges also drew attention to the timeline. Mishra’s husband died in 2021; she received gratuity and other retiral benefits in August 2022; and she opened the disputed FD only in 2025.

The court said SBI could potentially pursue a legal claim against Mishra as the deceased borrower’s legal heir, but such recovery would have to follow established legal procedure. It could not be carried out in an “arbitrary, capricious and whimsical manner”.

The judges were particularly critical of the movement of the FD between branches. They said the process “clearly indicates that the intention of the Bank was to achieve its purpose in a surreptitious manner.”
The court concluded: “The entire process is abominable and clearly an anathema to banking practice.”

SBI has been directed to return Rs 19,90,693 to Mishra with interest at the rate applicable to her fixed deposit within four weeks. It must also pay her Rs 1 lakh as exemplary and punitive compensation.

The writ petition was accordingly allowed. The petition was represented by advocates Syed Mohammad Haider Rizvi, Asheesh Kumar and Shakti Kumar Verma, while SBI and the other respondents were represented by advocate Anurag Srivastava.

title: If husband dies owing loan, can bank take money from his wife's FD? What Allahabad HC said in SBI case
